📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area.
  • In a recent development, so if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area. There are a few reasons for this. One is that permadraws are highly visible, turning a natural setting into an outdoor climbing gym. Permadraws also corrode rapidly in marine and coastal environments. Lastly, they are expensive.

In a recent development, so if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route? Leaving a carabiner is the next easiest solution. But what if you don’t want to do that?

It has been revealed that these nagging questions—as well as recent accidents—have compelled me to put together this long list of options for cleaning your next steep line. I’ve organized these methods into three categories:.

Each method has pros and cons in regards to simplicity, speed, and safety.

According to recent reports, ultimately, no single “best method” exists. Though there is a singular worst method: rappelling. Cleaning steep routes on rappel is a huge hassle for the climber, and bystanders on the ground who inevitably have to assist. Your method of choice will come down to the circumstances of each route and your personal preferences on simplicity, speed, and risk tolerance. Many of these methods are best saved for niche scenarios, or rare “if-then” situations. Still, it is best to be prepared with knowledge and equipment for those odd cleaning scenarios.

Below, I will discuss several methods for cleaning on the way up. I choose this approach if a route has a roof or dangerous swing potential or if, for whatever reason, I’m not ready to clean the route on the way down. Cleaning on the way up can take more time, but it brings safety gains. Methods range from simple to complex. If cleaning on the way down looks like a nuisance, just lower down to the ground and deal with it later (i.e., on the way back up).

If the route is well within the abilities of someone in your party, toproping to clean is always a good go-to. Never turn down a free toprope, right?

Issues with this method arise when the climbing gets hard enough where the climber might fall on toprope, thus becoming stuck in space. If the climber is unable to get back to the wall and decides to lower, then you may end up needing to re-lead the climb to re-clip the draws/directionals, so someone can attempt cleaning on toprope again. This is a huge pain, but I see it very often. Thankfully, there are many methods that can help you avoid this scenario.

Recent findings suggest that firstly, when someone is toproping to clean, we always say they must promise to get to the top. That way, they won’t leave the rope unclipped from lifesaving directionals. This reminder helps incentivize the climber to “proposal falls.” The worst time to fall is immediately after unclipping a bolt, when the swing will be the farthest, potentially leaving the climber stranded. If you think you might fall, it’s best to adequately rest hanging at a bolt before unclipping. Only unclip the bolt once you’re ready to charge to the next one.

What if you get unlucky and fall into space? You can try pulling on the belayer’s end of the rope if it’s within reach. However, this method is usually much less productive on steep topropes than on steep lead climbs. Oftentimes, pulling on the rope will get you nowhere.

Industry observers note that if pulling on the rope is getting you nowhere, the next method is boinking. Usually performed on lead, boinking is a strategy a leader can employ after falling into space and becoming unable to reach the rock or a rope. But it does work (albeit sometimes less effectively) on toprope. It’s also tiring and best for short stretches.

The boinking method is simple, but often executed inefficiently. The belayer takes tight on the rope, ideally, and hovers above the ground, or over an edge where they can hang their full body weight. Then, the climber does a pull-up on the climber side of the rope to create a loop of slack. When the climber rapidly releases the slack, the belayer drops. If the belayer is too low to the ground, they will hit the ground, and usually blame the climber.

Recent findings suggest that for maximum efficiency, the belayer can easily ascend the rope (using an ascender and their Grigri) the same distance that the climber needs to ascend. This obviates the need for timing the boinking/drops and is far more relaxing for both parties. It’s also far more efficient than the belayer jumping to take at the right time.

Recent findings suggest that an alternative to boinking is climbing the leash, as it’s called by highliners. This is the main method highliners use to climb the leash after falling, but also works identically in climbing scenarios when you’re not too far below your clip. If you’re flexible, place your heel above your tie-in knot, then pull on the rope, until you can straighten your leg and reach high for the wall. Once you pull on the wall or a draw, the belayer must rapidly take in all the extra slack.

Have the aforementioned methods become too tiring or inefficient? Or is there too much rope drag or rope stretch in the system for them to be effective? The next method is for the stuck climber to ascend the rope. If I don’t want to do the climbing again, I’ll usually jump straight to this method since I always have an ascender with me at the crag. If it’s just a short section to ascend, a prusik or other autoblock will work fine. But for cleaning a full route, you’ll thank yourself for bringing a proper ascender or at least nano-trax, to the crag (they weigh nothing).

In a recent development, if it is too difficult to pull in and release a draw, you can relocate your ascender above the draw, then clip a PAS/draw into the top carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. Slack the rope from your Grigri to unclip the rope from the draw. If you forgot to move the ascender above the clip, it will get stuck here. Begin ascending again until there is a 90-degree angle between your PAS and tensioned rope. The closer this angle is to 90 degrees, the less muscle required to pull in and unclip the draw. When you unclip the draw from the bolt, it stays attached to your PAS as you go swinging.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes rope shenanigans can get a bit clunky, especially in roofs. If the bolts are close enough together, you can implement some aid climbing techniques as needed. Sometimes it’s easier to ascend via yarding on bolts, and top-stepping in slings than jugging when it’s really steep. Just do whatever it takes to get up there and reclaim those draws! This can be done in a toprope scenario or a jugging scenario, with a slacked rope, or tensioned.

The biggest error when cleaning steep routes is cleaning on the way down, then taking a dangerous swing low on the route. There are many ways to clean on the way down. We’ll start with the standard scenario, then dive into niche techniques for oddball scenarios.

Many routes have an anchor just below the steep climbing. If this is the case, once you finish cleaning the steep terrain, the first step is to go off belay at that anchor and untie. Then pull the rope from above, re-tie in, and re-lower. When bolting routes, I love adding this type of anchor, not only to provide an easier, shorter version of the route, but also to greatly simplify the process of cleaning lower down the route.

The most common method for cleaning a steep sport route while lowering is to employ a trolley draw (it goes by many names). This draw connects the belay loop to the belayer’s side of the rope. As you lower, you can pull in on the belayer’s line to clean the draws. Higher up on the route, call for your belayer to hold (stop lowering) when the rope below your trolley draw is nearly level. Lower down on the route, you’ll want to stop sooner, just above the bolt.

There are a few methods for retrieving the draws, but whatever you do, be sure to stop and think before unclipping anything.

Recent findings suggest that the quickest method is to simply grab the wall, pull in (not up) to slack the draw and remove the draw from the bolt. If you can’t grab holds, often you can draw dyno: grab the draw with two hands and thrust in (not up) to momentarily slack the draw to remove it. In either of these cases, it is far more strenuous to remove the rope from the draw since your trolley draw will be yanking you away from the wall when you still have to clean the draw from the bolt. TLDR: If you’re tensioning the trolley, unclip the draw from the bolt.

If those methods aren’t working, go in direct to the draw you are hoping to retrieve. You can clip your PAS directly to the top carabiner of the draw. If using a draw to go direct, clip an additional draw from the belay loop to the lower carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. It’s best to resist the temptation to relocate the trolley draw into a tether draw. Note that if you remove your trolley draw and do not replace it, you could later unexpectedly fall into space or take a dangerous swing.

According to recent reports, once you’ve clipped direct to the draw, you can unclip the rope from the draw you wish to clean, calling slack if needed. Now, unlike other methods, the primary tension is no longer on the trolley, but instead directly on the bolt. Now pull down on the belayer’s rope to assist them in taking. That 90-degree rule applies here, too. Double check that your trolley is in place, assess the swing potential, then remove the draw from the bolt, and take the swing.

The lower you go on the route, the more potential energy—and extra rope—builds up in the system. If the trolley accidentally comes unclipped for any reason, it can be catastrophic. You could swing and hit a rock or a tree. The extra rope could even cause you to hit the ground. For this reason, as I get lower, I’ll often double-up my trolley draw. Why not?

Now let’s imagine we’ve lowered all the way down to the first bolt. As mentioned, the farther we end up from the plumb line, the higher the potential swing risk. Sometimes it is safe to unclip and take the swing. Other times, you might hit trees, rocks, or the ground. If both parties decide the swing is safe, the climber must first unclip the trolley draw before taking the swing. If you forget to unclip the trolley draw, you’ll drag the belayer along the ground as you swing. Very unpleasant!

Industry observers note that if the belayer is firmly anchored you can opt to keep the trolley draw in place to minimize the swing. However, since most sport crags don’t have convenient ground anchors, this option isn’t always possible. Just remember, don’t expect your belayer alone to stop your swing!

If you’re unsure whether a swing is safe, it’s usually best not to risk it. The horizontal distance of a swing is only a small part of understanding the potential impact. A giant King Swing can be perfectly safe, while a seemingly harmless three-foot swing can be devastating. The greater the starting angle of the swing, the more gravitational potential energy the climber has.

It has been revealed that once past the rope’s vertical plumb line (the lowest point of the swing), the climber begins losing speed. However, impact force depends just as much on how abruptly the climber is stopped as it does on their speed. Finally, account for rope stretch, which can increase the swing’s radius and lower the climber’s trajectory. Always make sure your swing won’t put you into the ground or another obstacle!

Even if the swing is all air, there can still be a risk of sharp rock cutting the rope. For this reason, it’s best to avoid big swings if the rope is rubbing rock. Usually, it’s the swing back toward the wall where rope damage is most likely to occur. Ropes cut most commonly from sideways grinding or sliding. If the rope must press rock, I prefer to place the rope where the rock is perpendicular to the rope’s force.

If a swing looks risky, the safest and easiest thing is to leave a draw or a carabiner. In my 20-plus years of sport climbing, I’ve never left a carabiner, but I do love this method because it’s allowed me to collect hundreds of free carabiners over the years, which I repurpose as lower-offs on anchors.

Besides cost, there are additional downsides to leaving gear. It is annoying to clip a bolt that has a bail carabiner. Numerous reported accidents exist wherein a climber falls after clipping a draw to the hanger over an existing carabiner, causing the draw’s carabiner to break. For this reason, people climbing after you should hopefully know to slide their draw between the carabiner and the wall when clipping.

On coastal routes, solid gate carabiners will eventually corrode shut, requiring a saw to remove. On the coast, only leave wiregates unless the wall is frequently trafficked. Speaking of difficult to remove, quick links should not be left on lead bolts. They require someone else to stop their climbing to use two hands to clean up after you. They are not cheaper than carabiners, unless you use the cheap hardware store ones that rust over and eventually require a saw to remove. If you must leave something, it must be a carabiner. Buy a stick clip and you’ll get an endless supply of free carabiners!

According to recent reports, let’s say we’ve decided to leave a draw. Now just stay connected with your trolley and continue lowering to the ground. The system will experience extra friction with the zigzag in the rope, which is nice. If you want to leave just a carabiner, you’ll go in direct to the draw you wish to clean, slack the rope, and clip the carabiner to the bolt above the draw. Then insert the climber’s end of the rope to the carabiner. Take hard, then remove the draw, and lower.

With both of these methods, you can still retrieve your draw/carabiner. The fastest, and sketchiest way to do so is to solo up to the first bolt (and back down). If it’s easy climbing and you’re comfortable, it does get the job done quickly. Otherwise, removing the draw with a stick clip is much safer, and won’t take too much longer.

Now let’s dig into a couple specialized scenarios.

According to recent reports, technically, the advice that follows on reclaiming the quickdraw from the first bolt safely is part of cleaning a route on the way down. But it involves some niche skills. So, let’s imagine you don’t want to leave a carabiner or draw behind on the first bolt. And you also don’t want to solo up to the first bolt, nor do you have a stick clip. If it’s a substantial, rounded glue-in, you can do a lower-out off the first bolt. In short, a lower-out is using a length of rope to do a secondary lower that safely equalizes the climber onto the plumb line. The goal here is to cancel out the swing potential, not to lower to the ground, so the belayer should hold tight. Do not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete or you’ll use up more rope on the lower-out than expected.

There are several ways to set up a lower-out. My favorite method? Give myself a huge tail on a figure-8 on a bight when cleaning the anchor. I make that tail double the length of the distance from the bolt to the object I might hit on a swing. When I arrive at that bolt, I go in direct. Then I unclip the trolley and ask my belayer to relocate under the anchor so they don’t swing. Once they’ve taken hard, I pass the extra long tail through the bolt, tension the extra tail, unclip my attachment to the bolt, lower myself out, then pull the rope through the bolt.

Sources indicate that lower-outs can be done with a knot on the end of the lower-out strand or without. Remember, you should always have the knot in the end of the belayer’s strand! Having a knot on the lower-out chord can keep you from lowering off the end and taking a bad swing if the chord comes up short. However, other times, skipping the knot can sometimes be safer (more on that in a minute). This is where stopping and analyzing is important.

According to recent reports, lower-outs can be done with and without a belay device. If it is a pure roof or horizontal traverse, I will use a belay device to lower-out as the forces are significant. This also puts a lot of friction (wear and tear) on the hangers, and should be done sparingly. If the angle is less extreme, I often prefer to lower-out by hand without a belay device. With this method, it is absolutely imperative that the belayer does not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete. Otherwise, the force on your hands will go from very comfortable to dangerous.

Recent findings suggest that but, why on earth would I ever prefer not using a belay device? If your lower-out chord is a tad short, finishing the lower-out by hand is often necessary to maximize your reach before letting go of the chord. The most dangerous option is to use a belay device and no knot; the issue being that it is very difficult to lower without your back facing the wall you’re trying to avoid hitting. Additionally, transitioning from lowering with the device to lowering by hand is risky. The safest thing is to knot the end, lower-out with an assisted braking belay device, hang on the device to clear the knot, then finish lowering by hand. If the pendulum angle is mild enough, I’ll skip those first steps and lower the whole way by hand.

If you use the lower-out method, make sure you have extra rope, as well as a knot in the belayer’s end of the rope. I’d recommend practicing lower-outs in no-risk scenarios first to understand the forces. You may be surprised how easy and safe it can be to two-hand the rope. After the lower-out, simply pull the rope to retrieve. If the belayer avoids lowering during the lower-out, the rope friction on the bolt is minimal and wear and tear on the bolt is non-existent. Still, it’s better to avoid making a habit out of this.

It has been revealed that but what if it’s not a fat rounded glue-in bolt? In that case, I’d highly recommend against a lower-out due to the rubbing of the rope on the sharper hanger. In this case, I would do a rappel-out. You’d rig it the same as a lower-out, but you set up your extra tail as a rappel instead of a lower (find the midpoint of your tail). Similarly, the belayer must avoid the temptation to lower.

While you are rappelling out, negligible rope pressure exists on the hanger, but you won’t create any tensioned rubbing friction like you would when lowering. When equalized onto the plumb line, you can pull the rope through the bolt hanger just like before. To further lessen any friction of the rope on the hanger while pulling, flick the tail and pull when the rope is lightest. This way, there will be no wear and tear.

Sources indicate that let’s say you weren’t planning to do a lower-out or rappel-out. Your belayer can toss you the bottom of the lead line to use just the same. Just make sure that before you untie the stopper knot at the end of the line, that the belayer ties a new stopper knot on their break strand (an overhand on a bight is fine). This requires a bit more rope than the first method, so just be careful.

But what if we don’t have enough rope for a lower-out and you don’t have the means to retrieve the draw any other way? If the bolt is solid, you can rappel straight through the bolt hanger. Blasphemy! This is clearly a last resort, but if you’re going to do it, you should at least know the best method. Firstly, never lower through a bolt hanger. That creates much more friction on the rope and bolt than a lower-out or pulling the rope after rappelling.

I personally do not believe pulling the rope after rappelling would cause any wear and tear, especially if it is a fatty rounded glue-in. What about an expansion bolt’s hanger? Recent tests have shown this scenario to hold around 11kN. There is some mild risk to the rope when pulling it due to the sharper edges. Just like the rappel-out, you can flick the end of the rope and pull the rope when it’s lightest. Additionally, having minimal extra rope to pull through the bolt is key. Rig the rope so its end barely touches the ground.

Lastly, avoid this technique above 15-20 feet off the ground unless it’s an emergency scenario because the rope weight will cause more friction when pulling. And of course, this can all be avoided with a stick clip.

If the bolts are close enough together, it’s often easier to just down-aid the route. The steeper the route, the less I’ll tension the rope. In a full roof with close enough bolts, I won’t tension the rope at all. There’s no need for bulky aiders though. I like to keep a 120cm sling coiled up on a lightweight carabiner permanently on my harness, using draws as a PAS.

If the route involves a full roof, it’s usually best to just down-lead/back-aid the route. This is the standard method with the massive roof cracks in Canyonlands. If you can bump cams then there’s no need to tension the rope.

However, this article is about sport climbing. What do you do in a pure roof with spaced out bolts? After running into this scenario many times, I find it easier to do a mix of toprope to clean and jugging the rope. I leave my Grigri on the rope, while the belayer belays with their Grigri, sometimes taking in slack, and sometimes acting as a meat anchor. A Black Diamond grappling hook on the bolt hanger allows me to easily unhook the bolt and take the swing.

In a recent development, speaking of getting creative, let’s wrap up with what will likely be one of the more controversial takes in this article. I’ve often found the fastest, safest (if you pay attention), and easiest (overall for the team) method is for the climber and belayer to both clean simultaneously. I can’t outright recommend it, unless you have a great attention to detail and years of experience with all of the previous techniques, as well as a variety of other techniques. But I’m including it for those climbing veterans who want to help their partners clean faster and easier.

Industry observers note that I generally jump to this method if cleaning the lower part of the route on the way down would be a nuisance or dangerous, but cleaning the top on lower is no-problem. First, I tie off the brake strand on my Grigri. Then, in order to lower the climber, I will climb up the route. I go up, they go down. In doing so, they cancel out much of my weight. If the climbing is hard, I’ll just jug up to the first bolt, clip in, and lower them to their next bolt. We both clean our respective bolts at our leisure. The only communication needed is for the climber to call the standard, “lower” and “hold.”.

The climber should stop cleaning one bolt before (above) entering any dangerous swing potential. Once they’ve hit that point, they just hang in space as the belayer continues to ascend with a mix of free, aid, and ascending as they clean. Of course, the belayer should tie backup knots when appropriate.

Once the belayer reaches that final draw left on the wall, they should double check that they are in fact above the danger swing potential and take the swing. If the belayer is still in the dangerous swing potential zone, they can use their brake strand to perform a lower-out. Then the belayer can lower themselves, and then the climber, to the ground. This method is fast and very efficient. It’s also nice for the tired climber who doesn’t want to clean the whole route. Just go about it very carefully and thoughtfully.

See? Cleaning steep routes doesn’t have to be a huge nuisance. If these techniques are all too much, just remember your safety comes first. Play it safe and leave a carabiner or a draw anytime. Yes, it’s not ideal, but carabiners are much cheaper than broken legs.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that in just over a week, two massive flooding events hit southwestern Colorado, destroying homes, businesses, and infrastructure across numerous mountain towns.
  • Sources indicate that “Rebuilding these damaged sections will not be quick, easy, or cheap,” Paul Talley, executive director of the Colorado Trail Foundation (CTF), remarked in a November 5 update on the floods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this article was updated on November 18, 2026, at 11:48 a.m. with additional information regarding the condition of the Colorado Trail section 28 and the Continental Divide Trail.

Industry observers note that in just over a week, two massive flooding events hit southwestern Colorado, destroying homes, businesses, and infrastructure across numerous mountain towns. But property is not all that the floods affected. Parts of both the Continental Divide Trail (CDT) and the Colorado Trail (CT) suffered damage that locals and trail organizations are calling “extensive” and “severe”, and which could take a very long time to repair.

Sources indicate that “Rebuilding these damaged sections will not be quick, easy, or cheap,” Paul Talley, executive director of the Colorado Trail Foundation (CTF), remarked in a November 5 update on the floods. “But we are committed to rebuilding.”.

In a recent development, as many of these areas are still inaccessible, there is very little confirmed information on their current state. Videos circulating online show missing bridges at key river crossings, and reports from the USFS and other agencies indicate that trailheads are damaged, and “heavy debris” is blocking some sections. But there has yet to be a full, official report on damage to these trails.

Here is what we know so far based on official updates, local reports, and videos.

Junction Creek is the CT’s southernmost section. Its trailhead, just outside of Durango, is also the CT’s southern terminus. Junction Creek Trail crosses multiple footbridges over the creek along its 19-mile stretch. A video posted to Instagram reveals the Junction Creek trailhead sign that many hikers use for their CT terminus photo now standing directly at the edge of a tall wash filled with flood debris.

“Junction Creek Trail #553 suffered a near-total loss in places where it parallels and crosses Junction Creek,” a USFS conditions report from November 13 reads. “Miles of trail as well as multiple bridges crossing Junction Creek were wiped out, replaced with massive piles of boulders, trees, and other flood debris.”.

According to the report, both the lowest trail bridge at 2.6 miles from the trailhead and the Walls Gulch Trail Bridge at 14.6 miles were destroyed. One social media video demonstrates the first footbridge washed away completely. The USFS posted its own video of the road to Junction Creek to Facebook, showing a “20-foot waterfall” over the edge of the destroyed road.

“There is no doubt that trails across the forest have suffered severe damage,” the San Juan National Forest wrote.

According to recent reports, in an interview with The Gazette, Talley said, “The Colorado Trail Foundation has never experienced an event that damaged this much trail. This is the largest section of trail ever damaged in our 52 years.”.

Recent findings suggest that authorities claim that recovery work will likely begin in spring and carry into summer 2027 due to weather. They discouraged hikers from even attempting to set out on the area’s trails.

“Record flooding across Southwest Colorado has left San Juan National Forest roads, trails, and other infrastructure inaccessible, severely damaged, and, in many cases, impassable,” a USDA Forest Service Facebook post reads. “Don’t become a statistic—rescue will not be readily available due to the current demand for search and rescue services.”.

The CTF said that it will be working over the winter with USFS, local partners, and volunteers to determine timelines and project budgets for the restoration efforts.

“It will be months before we can better understand what the next steps need to be on the sections damaged by climate events this season,” wrote Talley in his November 5 update.

There is even less information regarding damage to the CDT, which also passes through the flood-affected areas of Southwestern Colorado.

The Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC) posted on Facebook on October 23, warning hikers that flooding had made “travel to and from the CDT trailhead at Wolf Creek Pass impossible,” and that “hikers may need to make alternate aims to avoid the area.”.

On November 2, the CDTC posted another revision for CDT travelers. “The extent of damage to the CDT, access roads, and CDT communities is still unknown,” it noted. While the interactive map on its website shows no current closures of the trail due to flooding, the CDTC advised hikers to use “extreme caution and check with local authorities before visiting.”.

In a recent development, outside of Colorado, Newly introduced Mexico also experienced severe flooding. However, Audra Labert with the CDTC told Backpacker, “The area of New Mexico near the southern terminus did not experience significant damage from flooding.”.

While the full extent of the damage to these trails remains to be seen, what’s certain is that the CTF, CDTC, USFS, and other state agencies have a great deal of restoration work to do next summer. Volunteers will be in high demand, and Talley, of the CTF, promised to be open about how hikers can help.

Sources indicate that “While we do not yet know what it will take to rebuild, we do know what we will need,” Talley wrote. “We will need our supporters, we will need our dedicated volunteers, and we will need that community spirit that makes the CT so special.”.

I spend a lot of time outside. Unfortunately, a remarkable amount of the outdoors comes home with me.

Sources indicate that between my muddy hiking shoes, ski boots, camping gear, and two dogs who seem personally committed to bringing the entire Wasatch Range indoors, my floors take a beating. Dirt, gravel, pine needles, dog hair, the occasional stick. You name it, I’ve probably tracked it across my living room.

Recent findings suggest that for years, I accepted this as the price of admission. I swept. I vacuumed. I swept again. And then one of the dogs would come barreling through the door, and we’d start all over.

Which is why the best piece of outdoor gear I’ve bought this year has never actually been outside.

The Shark Navigator Robot Vacuum with Self-Emptying Base is presently on sale for $280, down from $450. It’s nearly identical to the model I’ve been using for the past six months, but with a larger self-emptying base that can hold up to 60 days of debris. With the holidays coming up, I think it might be one of the best gifts you could give someone who spends a lot of time outside, especially if they have dogs.

Sources indicate that I spent three years wavering over buying one. Surely I could manage to clean my own floors? Did I really need to spend hundreds of dollars on something I could do myself?

Recent findings suggest that for the past six months, my Shark has been dutifully making its rounds, picking up the dirt, debris, and dog hair that accumulate between adventures. It maps my house, works on carpet and hard floors, and returns to its dock to empty itself. I can schedule cleanings from my phone, so my floors get vacuumed while I’m outside doing something considerably more fun.

It’s not perfect. Occasionally it gets stuck, and once it even threw itself down the stairs. (I see you, adrenaline junkie!) But overall, it’s held up well to six months of living with two dogs and two humans who aren’t much better about tracking dirt inside.

The part I didn’t anticipate was how much joy I’d get from checking the collection bin.

I’m apparently so deeply into my mid-30s that one of the highlights of my day is seeing just how much dirt this little robot has collected.

ALL OF THIS WOULD BE ON MY FLOOR?

And now it’s not? And I didn’t have to clean it?

This thing isn’t going to put away my ski boots or haul me up the skin track. But it does mean I can spend less time cleaning up after my adventures and more time having them. And if that isn’t a great gift for someone who’d rather be outside, I don’t know what is.

Welcome, robot overlords. Have at it.

#9180. On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (875 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun.
  • Industry observers note that there is a cinema up north.
  • In a recent development, this is a film review of sorts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun. (Photo: Anton Korsun).

Industry observers note that there is a cinema up north. Beyond the rising northern star, beyond the Icefields Parkway, and far beyond the chaos and clamor of the Banff Mountain Film Festival—it is built in the image of a gothic cathedral and shrouded in storm. This cinema operates year round. It has no dress code, schedule, or rules on serving alcohol to minors. Inside, every visitor watches their own film: Some see triumph and elation. Others see despair, retreat, or a kaleidoscope of rock and ice before the front doors shut forever and the silver screen goes deathly black. Yet others simply stand alone in its great white hall, listening to the sound of silence and watching mountain ranges stretch to the horizon like limbs of a great white spider.

In a recent development, this is a film review of sorts. In September of 2026 I soloed Infinite Patience on the Emperor Face of Mount Robson. I’ve been asked to write about it. I’ve been asked why I haven’t posted anything on social media or pontificated my radness to the press. Frankly, it’s because I am a rather poor film critic.

There is no doubt in my mind that alpine climbing is more art than sport.

If I were to ask you—how did Usain Bolt run 100 meters in 9.58 seconds?

“Well, he moved his legs quite fast,” you might say.

It has been revealed that but can you tell me how Voytek Kurtyka and Robert Schauer suffered up the Shining Wall of Gasherbrum IV (7,925m) in a 10-day sleep-and-food-deprived push? Or how Steve House and Marko Prezelj clawed their way to the summit of the North Twin with one missing boot and two coreshot ropes? Because I can’t.

According to recent reports, I sit in awe of the performers on stage as they pull another rabbit from their hats or escape the icy chains of some far-flung north face yet again. The beauty of alpinism is similar to the beauty of theater, dance, and stage magic—an illusion of wizardry brought about by true mastery of the performers.

According to recent reports, however, while similar, alpinism and theater are not the same. Climbing has no audience and no stage. Climbing media has both. In recent times it has become too easy to convince ourselves that perception equals participation—that by clicking that “follow” button or watching that film we can stand in the shoes of the artist. But we can’t. Because to believe otherwise would be to mistake climbing as performing art for climbing as performance art. The former is the way the ascent is portrayed in words, photographs, or film. The latter—what was seen, felt, thought and feared in the moment—is privy only to the performers themselves.

It has been revealed that I often find myself wondering about how the way an ascent is communicated influences the audience’s perception of what actually happened. This can range from flying in a massive-budget film crew, to more subtle cues, like how a photo was cropped for Instagram, or whether one was shared at all. These words themselves are guilty, although I try to segregate my act of climbing from my act of writing about it.

In a recent development, my reluctance to share much about the climb stems from a fear that this blade is sharp on both sides—that the audience’s media-driven perception can in turn influence the climber’s own perception of the experience. Much like how the behaviour of quantum particles changes when they’re observed, climbers too, change our behaviour. Our egos feed off validation. Our eye becomes drawn to the viewfinder or to the stopwatch. We feel the presence of the audience cut through the ridgetop wind. We hear their applause over the crash of séracs in the distance.

I watched The Alpinist on the substantial screen when it was first released. While I never met Marc-André Leclerc, it left me feeling that much more went unsaid—that the real movie of his life was seen through his eyes only. A movie no one can rewind.

But anything is possible in cinema. In his account of Infinite Patience, Marc-André describes being unable to take a photo of a beautiful sunrise because his camera batteries had failed—“the shadow of Mt. Robson extending forever into the horizon against a red sky.”.

Recent findings suggest that from my sleeping perch high on the Emperor Ridge, I awoke to the same scene. Waves of red and gold crashed against the east face of Whitehorn Mountain while Robson’s summit pyramid shadowed the valley thousands of feet below. Was this movie magic or something more? Feeling as if I was suddenly not alone, I pulled out my phone in disbelief and took that photo. We can’t rewind each other’s films, but sometimes life lets us watch them together.

In a recent development, nonetheless, I’m saddened to be left alone with my experience. My words are a lousy companion and my photographs are only worth a thousand lousy words. All I know is that I watched my film on the summit of Mount Robson. Where are you watching yours?

Industry News: The 9 Best Snowshoes of 2027

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

  • If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Bean Pathfinder BOA Rec Snowshoe Package.
  • Industry observers note that after a season of snowshoe-testing in blizzards, sub-zero temps, and alpine ice, our top pick is the MSR Revo Explore ($290) for its light weight, flexibility, and impressive grip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that L.L. Bean Pathfinder BOA Rec Snowshoe Package.

Retrospec Drifter Lightweight Snowshoes.

Industry observers note that after a season of snowshoe-testing in blizzards, sub-zero temps, and alpine ice, our top pick is the MSR Revo Explore ($290) for its light weight, flexibility, and impressive grip. Looking for a crazy-affordable pair that will last for years? The Retrospec Drifter Lightweight Snowshoes ($50-70) are nearly bulletproof, easy to manipulate with gloves on, and provide a full feature set. This year we added the L.L. Bean Pathfinder Snowshoe Package (Best Snowshoe Package) and Atlas Montane ($250) (Best for Deep Snow.).

It has been revealed that snowshoes are some of the oldest winter gear known to humankind—the tech literally has prehistoric origins, with rudimentary versions dating back nearly 6,000 years ago. Today, the top ‘shoes boost flotation, grip, and ease of use, all while shaving weight. Over the years, our testers have tried hundreds of models in waist-deep drifts, through wet, cement-like snow, and on steep, icy slopes, all in the name of narrowing down the top of the class. Here are the best snowshoes of 2027.

Sizes: 22, 25 in Weight: Men’s: 3.8 lbs (22 in), 4.1 lbs (25 in); Women’s: 3.6 lbs (22 in), 3.9 lbs (25 in) Maximum Load: Men’s: 180 lbs (22 in), 220 lbs (25 in); Women’s: 180 lbs (22 in), 210 lbs (25 in).

Pros and Cons + Excellent traction + Easy-to-engage heel lift + Very secure binding – Pricey.

The Revo Explore snowshoes from MSR have been a tester favorite for over a decade: They’re lighter, more flexible, and grippier than most snowshoes on the market today. Credit a hybrid construction, which combines a tough, injection-molded plastic decking with a jagged-edged steel frame and pivoting toe crampon. The 2026 model keeps last year’s newly introduced binding—the TPU rubber stretch mesh Paradigm—which continues to impress testers with its security and comfort. The ridged, steel frame boosts side traction, while the two front toe crampons and a small, tooth-lined crossbar provide enough bite to stick to icy hills and steep ravines. Our Oregon tester reached for them in everything from deep powder to spring crust in Eastern Oregon’s Wallowa and Blue Mountains—when other people weren’t using them. “My husband makes fun of snowshoeing (he’s a skier) and claims to hate it, but I caught him happily using this pair,” she stated.

Sizes: 20.5, 22.5, 26.5 in Weight: 3.6 lbs (20.5), 3.8 lbs (22.5), 4lbs (26.5) Maximum Load: 180 lbs (20.5 in), 260 lbs (22.5 in), 300 lbs (26.5 in).

Pros and Cons + Excellent grip + Comfortable stride + Tall heel lift – Expensive.

Industry observers note that the Highlander Instinct takes the snowshoe crampon and dials it up to 11. Most snowshoes have a basic underfoot crampon for some traction on slopes, and a few brands add teeth around the edges. The Highlander Instinct uses a stainless steel crampon under the toe that’s as long and sharp as some mountaineering crampons we’ve used, plus lateral grips around the edge of the chassis and mini serrated grip bars at strategic grip points across the platform. Over three days of steep, icy hills in Rocky Mountain National Park, our tester didn’t slip once, aided, in part, by the easy-to-use heel lifts. The rockered profile and wasp-waist shape allow a natural stride and help the crampons bite, no matter the incline. That narrow waist and tapered tail kept these easy to walk in, too, without the waddling common in most wider snowshoes. They floated well in a few inches of upcoming snow, but drifts of more than a foot proved challenging. The BOA bindings were easy to adjust even with bulky gloves, and once dialed in proved extremely comfortable and secure.

Sources indicate that sizes: 25, 30, 36 in. (men’s) 21, 25 (women’s) Weight: 4.9 lbs (25 in), 5.6 lbs (30 in), 6.5 lbs (36 in) Maximum Load: 200 lbs (25 in), 250 lbs (30 in), 280 lbs (36 in).

Pros and Cons + Great traction on hills + Easy to adjust, glove-friendly binding + Wide range of sizes – Wider decks can be cumbersome.

L.L. Bean’s Pathfinder snowshoe package impressed beginners and experts alike among this year’s Rocky Mountain test team. The BOA bindings—not often found in beginner-friendly packages—were a fan favorite, snugging quickly over mountaineering boots and casual snowboots and never needing another adjustment. The bindings were easy to use while wearing gloves and mittens, a massive plus on a trip to Rocky Mountain National Park’s Emerald Lake where the windchill dropped to -20 degrees.

On a windy, late-season day in the Indian Peaks, the crampons easily bit into steep ice crust in the morning, and the decks—made of high-density polyethylene—floated over thick corn snow in the afternoon. The poles are sturdy aluminum and adjust with an external lever lock that never failed or stuck. The only con was the width of the frame, which occasionally snagged on willow tips and low-hanging branches. But once in the open powder above treeline, the wider area underfoot became a plus. If you want a sturdy set of snowshoes and poles that holds up in most winter conditions, the Pathfinder Package delivers.

Sizes: 22, 25 in. Weight: 3.8 lbs (22 in), 4 lbs (25 in) Maximum Load: 180 lbs (22 in), 210 (25 in).

Pros and Cons + Good traction on slopes + Easy-to-use binding + Heel lift – Expensive.

Many snowshoes are unisex, which means they tend to be too substantial for lighter folks who don’t need the oversized frame. The women’s-specific Lightning Ascents are nearly an inch narrower and five ounces lighter than the men’s version, making them perfect for smaller people with narrow gaits. The Ascent’s binding, a comfortable rubber mesh toe cup that secures via two rubber side straps that buckle into place, is simple to use with just a quick two-handed pull. The tooth-lined stainless steel frame and pivoting, two-pronged toe crampons impressed on outings in Rocky Mountain National Park’s Glacier Gorge, where our 5’4”, 115-pound tester tackled icy sidehills and slippery windcrust. But the Lightning Ascent isn’t just ideal for smaller snowshoers: Our 5’10”, 155-pound tester also found the precise, narrow ‘shoe design useful while climbing the gullied slopes of northern Vermont.

Industry observers note that sizes: 20.5, 23.5, 27 in. Weight: 3.6 lbs (20.5 in), 3.8 lbs (23.5 in), 4 lbs (27 in) Maximum Load: 180 lbs (20.5 in), 260 lbs (23.5 in), 300 lbs (27 in).

Pros and Cons + Intuitive BOA system + Multi-direction crampons + Flexible + Heel lift – Expensive – No tail extensions – Not great in powder.

According to recent reports, for those who loathe fiddly snowshoe bindings, the Symbioz Hyperflex Instinct is a godsend. While several snowshoes incorporate BOA closures into their design, few are quite as simple as the Instinct’s. The design: a single knob that tightens the toe, sides, and heel using interlinked cables that run through the perimeter of the binding, eliminating any and all trailhead exasperation. It takes fewer than 10 seconds to step into and secure the snowshoe, but the Instinct stayed glued to our boots all day long, even while walking on bumpy, uneven terrain in Colorado’s Indian Peaks Wilderness. Another characteristic we loved: flexible decking made of injection-molded polypropylene. The pliable material gave us just enough torsional flexibility to enhance comfort and reduce ankle-twisting on uneven surfaces. While sidehilling through a labyrinth of postholes in Rocky Mountain National Park, eight lateral stainless steel teeth kept our Colorado tester upright and stable.

Size: 25 in Weight: 2.2 lbs (Tru Trak bindings), 2.4 lbs (Spin Bindings) Maximum Load: 215 lbs.

Pros and Cons + Lightweight + Easy-to-use BOA-style bindings – Below-average traction – No heel lift.

Over a pound lighter than the next-lightest snowshoes in our test, the Elite Race Ultralights, designed for endurance and adventure races, delivered on their name. Even with ultralight bindings and minimalist crampons, these snowshoes impressed testers with their durability. The PU-coated nylon mesh decking and aluminum alloy frame stood up to rock-studded snow slopes and scraped across ice with barely any sign of wear. Our testers loved them for their comfort and ease of use; thick foam padding around the binding straps eliminated hot spots, and once set, they stayed on without further adjustment. The narrow tails let you walk—or run—with your normal stride. One tester taught several Avalanche Terrain Avoidance classes for the Colorado Mountain Club in these snowshoes, where their ease of use and float in five inches of fresh snow was the envy of all her students. There is a cost to mild crampons and the simple plastic ridges on the perimeter frame: The Ultralights gripped well on moderate slopes, but skidded a bit on steep ice.

Sizes: 21, 25, and 30 in. Weight: 4 lbs (21 in), 4.2 lbs (25 in), 4.8 lbs (30 in) Maximum Load: 120-250 lbs.

Pros and Cons + Very affordable + Convenient, effective heel lift + Glove-friendly bindings – Heavy.

The updated version of our perennial budget pick, the Retrospec Drifter, impressed with good flotation, comfortable heel lifts for hills, and glove-friendly bindings.

The double ratchet strap bindings proved secure, intuitive, and easy to adjust, with buckles that were large enough to be manipulated without removing our gloves. The heel lift was ideal for 30-degree slopes in Rocky Mountain National Park, and was much easier to flip up or down—even with gloves on—than last year’s model. For a shoe that costs less than a quarter of some of our other winners, that’s an impressive feature set.

Plus, the Drifter is just about as bulletproof as a snowshoe gets: The one-piece polypropylene deck and aluminum alloy frame didn’t show a scratch from early-season rocks, surprise tree roots, and a long rattly drive in a roof box full of pointy gear.

Industry observers note that our Colorado testers found the underfoot crampons perfect for hard snow in the Indian Peaks, but with only six main crampons beneath the toes and no teeth around the perimeter, anything steeper than a 20-degree slope felt pretty sketchy when iced over. The Drifters also aren’t particularly strong in the flotation department: Our five-foot-four tester, who used the shorter 21-inch version, struggled to stay afloat the most.

But for $50, these snowshoes pack plenty of great features into an adventure-ready, accessible package.

Size: 22 in Weight: 3.6 lbs Maximum Load: 180 lbs.

Pros and Cons + One size fits all + Affordable + Impressive traction + Float tail-compatible – No heel lift.

Described by testers as “aggressively sturdy,” these near-unbreakable injection-molded snowshoes will get you where you want to go with minimal fuss and fear of equipment failure. The stiff plastic body doesn’t have a lot of flex to match a hiker’s gait, but was ideal for packing down the trail for our Oregon-based tester’s three adventuring huskies.

Industry observers note that the Evo Trail’s serrated steel traction rails, four-toothed toe crampons, and plastic, anti-slide ridges kept our testers upright, even on crusty sidehills. Flotation is great, too, for such a small snowshoe. One of our Pacific Northwest-based testers took the Evo Trails through 20 miles of deep, unconsolidated snow in Oregon’s Blue Mountains and stayed on top of the powder the entire time—no easy feat in the chilly, snowbound region.

This year’s model uses the brand’s Paraglide binding, which combines a wide piece of stretch mesh over the toe with a simple heel strap. They climb decently well without a heel lift, though we think it should be a standard feature, even on this entry-level ‘shoe.

Sizes: 23, 27 in (women’s), 25, 30, 35 in (men’s) Weight: 4.3 lbs (25 in), 4.7 lbs (30 in), 5 lbs (35 in) Maximum Load: 160 lbs (23 in), 200 lbs (27 in), 200 lbs (25 in), 250 lbs (30 in), 300+ lbs (35 in).

Pros and Cons + Great float + Heel lift + Good traction on hills – Bindings can be fiddly.

The Atlas Montane’s lightweight PVC decking and an aluminum tube frame combine for a classic deep-powder snowshoe. Our six-foot-two, 200-pound Colorado tester took the 30-inch version for a winter ascent of Longs Peak and floated easily over two to three feet of new snow, even with a pack full of heavy climbing gear. Even the smaller decks (down to 23 inches) wowed our testers with easy traverses of powdery alpine meadows and serious forest drifts. Underfoot crampons and carbon steel lateral grips at the snowshoe’s midpoint kept footing sure and steady even on icy sidehills.

The Montane is wider than most of the other snowshoes we tested in both the men’s and women’s models, which gives this ‘shoe its superior flotation, but it does take a moment to adapt your gait and stop banging the snowshoes together. Our testers found the strap bindings fiddly with thick ski gloves on, but once the two straps were latched in place, they stayed there for the whole trip. On powder days, the flotation more than makes up for the simple, slightly inconvenient binding. If you’re planning off-trail travel in deep snow, especially if you’ll be carrying heavy overnight packs, these are the snowshoes for you.

Flat, uncomplicated terrain doesn’t require too much from a pair of snowshoes. Simple, comfortable bindings and a deck that provides adequate flotation are all you need. If icy slopes or deep snow aren’t in your future, save money with a budget pair made from heavier molded plastic and less aggressive traction.

Industry observers note that on the other end of the spectrum are snowshoes built for challenging terrain—slushy hills, narrow singletrack, or mixed rock and ice. A secure wrap around the heel and/or multiple straps along the foot are important for stability. Quick binding systems, like those that utilize a BOA twist lock, are helpful when taking snowshoes on and off in precarious terrain and a huge time-saver compared with fiddly three-strap setups. Snowshoes geared towards mountainous ascents will have a wider variety of spikes and crampons underfoot—and in more abundance—to offer grip both horizontally and laterally, and to bite through different types of ice. A heel lift that provides about 2 inches of lift (that’s easy to flick open and closed with either gloved hands or a trekking pole) is a must for giving your feet and calves an assist on the steeps.

According to recent reports, in deep, fresh powder, you’ll want wider, longer snowshoes (or those that come with extensions) for superior flotation. On the flipside, if you’re headed out on a weight-conscious backpacking trip and/or plan to strap the snowshoes to your pack for much of the trip, prioritize lightweight construction, like a pair made from aluminum and TPU-coated nylon, for reducing fatigue on-foot and outside your pack.

Industry observers note that over the past several years, our veteran testers braved blizzards, sub-zero temps, and icy alpine climbs to find out which snowshoes are really the best. Only nine models stood up to the rigors of our testing to earn a spot on this list.

In a recent development, we looked at design, features, ease of use, comfort, traction, cost, weight, and flotation in deep snow to narrow down the best of the best from the current market. This year, some tried-and-tested snowshoe models received updates, like new bindings and decking materials, which we then reevaluated. Others haven’t changed through the years: their simple designs and technologies have withstood the test of time.

Recent findings suggest that kristin Smith A former Backpacker editor, category manager Kristin Smith has been a full- or part-time mountain guide for most of the last decade. In her spare time, she teaches Avalanche Terrain Avoidance for the Colorado Mountain Club, guides clients through the nearby peaks of Rocky Mountain National Park, and maps out fresh places to visit with her recently-acquired pilot’s license.

Jill Yarger Jill Yarger works as a mountain guide in Boulder, Colorado. She moved for an engineering job, found the mountains, and never left; that was almost 40 years ago. Since then she’s spent 13 years volunteering in the Rocky Mountain Rescue Group, joined the National Ski Patrol and Mountain Rescue Associations, and climbed in Alaska, Italy, and Canada.

Jessica Bucklin Jessica Bucklin spent a decade sailing tall ships all over the world before moving to the coast of Maine, where finding enough snow to snowshoe often requires just a walk down the road. When she’s not exploring Maine’s mountain parks she captains a towboat out of Bath.

Joe O’Leary Joe’s guiding career spanned North, Central, and South America before he settled in Colorado, where he now trains other guides in whitewater rafting, mountain biking, backpacking, and leadership development. When he’s not biking, rafting, or kayaking, he works as a nature photographer and writer.

Supermoon Season Is Coming. Here’s Where to Watch in Every Single State.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3188 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanksgiving week will bring the first supermoon since January 2026.
  • Sources indicate that I’ve chased at least a dozen supermoons as an astrophotographer and night-sky tourist, from the badlands of South Dakota to Serengeti National Park in Tanzania.
  • The Thanksgiving-week supermoon will hit on Tuesday, November 24 It reaches full illumination that morning, but there’s an even better time to view it: sunset.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving week will bring the first supermoon since January 2026. It kicks off a series of not one but four oversized full moons in a row, including the closest supermoon of the decade thus far in December. While you can admire the bright sphere throughout the night, a few specific tips and tricks will dramatically improve your view—including strategizing when and where to watch.

Sources indicate that I’ve chased at least a dozen supermoons as an astrophotographer and night-sky tourist, from the badlands of South Dakota to Serengeti National Park in Tanzania. In this guide, I’m sharing everything you need to know as we enter supermoon season, including timing logistics and guidance on where to watch the luminous sphere in every state.

The Thanksgiving-week supermoon will hit on Tuesday, November 24 It reaches full illumination that morning, but there’s an even better time to view it: sunset.

According to recent reports, the round orb looks especially large and bright as it rises and sets due to an effect known as the moon illusion. A supermoon can appear up to 30 percent brighter and 14 percent bigger than the smallest full moon. Near the horizon, it looks even more gargantuan. If you’re hoping to snag supermoon photos, moonrise and moonset are the times to do it.

The full moon rises in the east to northeast as the sun sets in the west, and sinks in the west as the morning sun appears out east. The golden hour hues only add to the drama, turning the globe a tangerine tinge.

The last two supermoons of 2026 line up perfectly with holiday-season gatherings. In addition to a Thanksgiving-week event on November 24, we also have a full supermoon right before Christmas on December 23. It’s the closest full moon we’ve witnessed yet this decade, at 221,667 miles away.

After December, we have two more supermoons in early 2027: January 22 and February 20. You can use the following locations to watch these or any future supermoons, since moonrise and moonset locations remain relatively the same all year.

It has been revealed that while the supermoon looks stellar during both moonrise and moonset, I’m especially partial to its ascension because it doesn’t come with an early wake-up call. The full moon’s first appearance coincides with sunset. And soon after it rises, I can begin spotting a few constellations.

With that in mind, here are the best places to watch the rising supermoon in every state. Remember: These locations are just starting points. You can absolutely watch the magic beyond this list. Just scout a viewpoint with relatively unobstructed vistas to the east, where the evening moon first highlights.

Sources indicate that pair supermoon watching with thick forest overlooks in Cheaha State Park, set 70 miles east of Birmingham. Out here, you can watch the crater-pocked orb rise from Alabama’s tallest point, Bunker Tower at around 2,400 feet. The simultaneously setting sun will turn the hardwood landscapes into varying shades of peach and pink.

According to recent reports, watch the supermoon ascend over mountain-flanked Kachemak Bay from the east-facing side of the Homer Spit, a thin sliver of land crossing 4.5 miles into the waterway. This glacier-carved landmass provides two-for-one awe; watch the sun set in the west and the moon rise out east. If you’re lucky, the northern lights could follow, too.

According to recent reports, catch the eye-popping supermoon rising above one of America’s most famed landmarks, the Grand Canyon. Mather Point’s east-facing view provides the perfect vantage point, although you’ll have numerous other lookouts to scout from, including Yaki Point and Shoshone Point, or further in the canyon along the South Rim trail. (Just read ahead on travel restrictions given recent flooding closures.).

Head slightly west of Little Rock for one of Arkansas’ best supermoon viewpoints: Pinnacle Mountain State Park. The getaway’s visitor center is a popular spot for sunrise, which makes it great for moonrise, too.

Sources indicate that death Valley is about as otherworldly as national parks get, even more so with a supersized moon rising above its surrounding peaks. Watch for the sphere above the badlands from Zabriskie Point, or head to Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes to marvel as it inches above the Grapevine peaks.

Perched above Boulder, the Colorado Chautauqua—a hub for arts, culture, and outdoor adventure—provides the perfect supermoon view. The earliest portion of the Chautauqua Trail, including the trail overlook, provides unobstructed glimpses to the east. For an easier vista, spot it right from Chautauqua Park. Don’t miss the sun setting behind the snowy Flatirons to the west, too.

From Hammonasset Beach State Park’s boardwalk and shoreline, you can peer back and forth from the east’s supermoon to the west’s sunset, with the Long Island Sound in your foreground. Head to the park’s southern end, Meigs Point, for the most panoramic view. The beach is just over 20 miles east of New Haven.

According to recent reports, the Point in Cape Henlopen State Park, where the Delaware Bay meets the Atlantic, offers another 360-degree supermoon and sunset perch. You can watch the moon crawl above the ocean as the sun dips beneath the bay and, if you situate yourself correctly (about one-third of the way up the west-side beach), behind the Delaware Breakwater East End Lighthouse. East-facing Rehoboth Beach just south of here is another stellar supermoon spot.

In a recent development, barrier island Key Biscayne offers over a mile of east-facing beachfront perfect for catching the supermoon. Head to the Cape Florida Beach at Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park to enjoy it while watching for dolphins or visiting the Cape Florida Lighthouse; the park is within ten miles of downtown Miami.

For supermoon views with a surreal foreground, head to Jekyll Island’s east coast. Here, you’ll find Driftwood Beach, a waterfront made famous by its graveyard of gnarled oaks and pines. The lunar views continue down the coastline, including public access points like the South Dunes Picnic Area and Great Dunes Park. Or, join a Jekyll Island Dolphin Tour to swoon over the rising moon while scouting for cetaceans.

With miles upon miles of scenic east-facing coastlines, the options for supermoon watching in Hawaii run the gamut. Try Pololū Valley on the Island of Hawaii for the chance to see our neighboring space rock as well as migrating whales, which visit the area from December to April. Catch it from the elevated overlook, or via a hike down to the waterfront.

For a sky-high vista, stroll the pedestrian sidewalks on Perrine Memorial Bridge in Twin Falls, Idaho, just as the sun sets and the supermoon appears. Make sure to walk the east side to catch the lunar marvel above the Snake River, which runs over 1,000 miles from Wyoming to Washington state.

Sources indicate that downtown Chicago’s 18-mile lakefront pedestrian and bike trail is situated perfectly for a supermoon ascent. The route, located on the city’s east side, offers countless vantage points. Peer moonward from North Avenue Beach, the end of Navy Pier, or the viewpoint just behind Adler Planetarium.

Brown County State Park, nicknamed the Little Smokies, is the largest park in Indiana—and one of the best places in the state for seeing the supermoon. Drive up to the Hesitation Point overlook. It’s a local favorite for sunrise, which makes it perfect come supermoon season.

Stare slack-jawed as the supermoon rises above the Wisconsin River and the Mississippi from Pikes Peak State Park, one of Iowa’s best outdoor getaways. Viewpoints like the Pikes Peak Scenic Overlook are reachable by car, although you can get water-view hikes along the park’s 11.5 trail miles. It’s around 100 miles from Cedar Rapids.

Industry observers note that the closer you can spot the supermoon to the horizon, the better, and Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve’s vast and flat fields do the trick. From the preserve’s scenic routes, such as Southwind Nature Trail, you can admire the lunar wonder along with potential bison, deer, and hare. The destination, part of the world’s largest remaining tallgrass prairie landscape, is 75 miles southwest of Topeka.

Sources indicate that see the supermoon soar above the Appalachians from Pine Mountain State Resort Park in eastern Kentucky. The destination’s one-mile Chained Rock Trail leads you to a favorite local sunrise spot, gaining around 250 feet of elevation via stairs and packed dirt. Keep watch for wildlife like bears while you’re out here.

It has been revealed that any supermoon view will delight, but watching the orange orb reflect off water is especially enchanting. For that, try Louisiana’s Lake Martin, roughly 50 miles west of Baton Rouge. Fantastical cypress trees dot the water body, with frequent avian sightings from egrets to spoonbills. You can admire the scenery from the five-mile Levee Trail, or via kayak or boat.

Few coastal landmarks are as recognizable as Portland Head Light, a 1790s-era lighthouse perched atop Maine’s craggy coast. From here, sky-watchers can enjoy unobstructed views to the east—excellent for a sunrise or, soon, a supermoon. The lookout is six miles from downtown Portland.

According to recent reports, from North Point State Park, you can watch the supermoon ascend above the country’s largest estuary, Chesapeake Bay. Get your legs moving on the park’s four-mile Hiker-Biker Trail, then watch the pockmarked moon appear from Crystal Pier or its adjacent beach.

Hear the crashing waves as you watch the peachy moon travel above the Atlantic. Halibut Point State Park provides a multisensory experience, complete with the scent of sea spray on the 440-million-year-old granite rocks. For the best viewpoint, head to the park’s northern tip, where you can look east to watch the supermoon and west to admire the plummeting sun.

Detroit’s 982-acre Belle Isle provides ample moon-viewing coordinates, all with the Detroit River as your backdrop. Hit the northeast section of the Belle Isle’s Driker Trail for the most unobstructed vista.

Industry observers note that perched atop a 130-foot cliff, Split Rock Lighthouse in northern Minnesota comes with serious supermoon potential—and, if you’re lucky, a chance to see the northern lights. To watch the moonrise down at lake level, make a detour to adjacent Pebble Beach.

Sardis Lake, which is actually an over 98,000-acre reservoir set 60 miles south of Memphis, provides numerous supermoon vantage points. Watch the moon soar above this beloved fishing hole at the end of Pats Bluff or from the John W. Kyle State Park Campground.

In a recent development, see the supermoon’s first appearance from America’s smallest national park, Gateway Arch. This east-facing getaway has the perfect photo-composition recipe: if you’re standing in the right place (west of the arch), you can photograph the moon rising beneath the 630-foot colossus.

According to recent reports, visit the west side of glassy Flathead Lake to watch the lunar globe wow above the Mission Mountains. Stop-offs like West Shore, Big Arm, and Volunteer Park offer stunning vistas that are especially quiet come winter. If time allows, detour up to Glacier National Park just under 60 miles to the north.

Standing Bear Lake, located 20 miles from downtown Omaha, offers a unique urban vantage point on the roughly four-mile paved Standing Bear Lake Loop trail. Alternatively, try Omaha’s Glenn Cunningham Lake, with a variety of overlooks and campgrounds on the water body’s western side.

Head to the crimson crags of otherworldly Valley of Fire State Park. From the 1.5-mile Fire Wave Trail or the route’s scenic turnaround point, you can spot the supermoon above the sandstone. Other good moon-watching routes in this park, set around 50 miles from Las Vegas, include the Balanced Rock Trail and White Domes.

Fresh Hampshire’s largest lake delivers a variety of supermoon vantage points. Try the Lincoln Park waterfront or the 1.5-mile route up Mount Major, a challenging ascent that leads to the 1,786-foot summit with granite balds and 360-degree views.

Industry observers note that pair the supermoon with the Statue of Liberty or Manhattan skyline for scale at Liberty State Park, one of New Jersey’s most scenic public spaces. Hit the roughly two-mile waterfront walk for the best overlooks in this Jersey City park. It’s near the tail end of the 18-mile Hudson River Waterfront Walkway, which runs from the George Washington Bridge to Bayonne.

According to recent reports, sunset is one of White Sands National Park’s most popular moments, and for good reason. Golden hour turns this typically snow-white gypsum sand a mosaic of blush and tangerine hues. The landscape gets even more magical with a supermoon to top it off. You can catch the show throughout the dune system, particularly along the Alkali Flat Trail; just leave ample time to hike in and out, and note that the park closes 30 minutes after sunset.

Few destinations are as perfect for this winter’s two holiday supermoons as Lake Placid, particularly along the western side of Mirror Lake. The quaint mountain town goes all out with festive décor and winter fun, including bobsledding and ice skating. Meanwhile, you can see the supermoon reflect off of Mirror Lake from several overlooks, including Mid’s Park.

With its position along the Atlantic Coast, the Outer Banks boasts supermoon sightings galore. Hatteras Island wows with some of the area’s most impressive scenery, including the black-and-white-striped lighthouse circa 1870 and easily reachable beaches like Cape Point.

It has been revealed that theodore Roosevelt National Park is known for many things: its free-ranging bison, badlands scenery, and potential contiguous U.S. northern lights views. This winter, add a supermoon to the mix, particularly along the park’s scenic stop-offs like Badlands Overlook and Skyline Vista.

In a recent development, ohio is another great place to pair lunar wonder with lighthouse explorations. Marblehead Lighthouse State Park, located right along Lake Erie, faces east for sunrise and, on lucky nights, a supermoon. This is the Great Lakes’ oldest continually operated lighthouse; it was first lit in 1822.

Visit the 2,500-acre Lake Hefner near Oklahoma City for supermoon wonder in the Sooner State. The Bert Cooper Trail loops you around the lake for roughly nine paved miles; the best lunar sightseeing awaits on the west side, including Lakeshore Park.

The 16,000-square-foot Pittock Mansion brims with history, but that’s not all that’s on offer here. Pittock Mansion comes with one of the best views of Portland out to Mount Hood—all facing east. That means you could see the supermoon rising above the city, with the snowcapped 11,249-foot colossus in the distance. The grounds stay open into the evening, although mansion tours are limited to the daytime.

A hook of land juts out into Lake Erie from northern Pennsylvania, and it’s one of the state’s best spots for supermoon spotting. The getaway, Presque Isle State Park, is just four miles outside of downtown Erie. The National Natural Landmark comes with numerous east-facing vistas, from the sprawling beach to Gull Point Observation Deck (reachable via a 1.5-mile hike).

In a recent development, many come to Newport for the Cliff Walk’s mansions, but the trail’s east-facing views promise incredible supermoon lookouts, too. Start at The Breakers and stroll north toward Forty Steps or beyond. You’ll have a number of views to choose from en route, not to mention a glimpse of the lives of Rhode Island’s rich and famous.

Recent findings suggest that for a South Carolina supermoon show, visit Folly Island, a roughly seven-mile barrier island that’s located about 10 miles outside of Charleston. The getaway’s public beaches make it easy to admire that scenic space rock. Try Folly Beach County Park for a land-based evening, or join a sunset boat tour from the island for the chance to see cetaceans beneath the shining orb.

Another otherworldly supermoon scene awaits in Badlands National Park. Stop-offs like Bigfoot Pass Overlook and Panorama Point look east across the park’s striated landscapes. Get a unique moon glimpse on the Door Trail, a short boardwalk that leads to a rugged and east-facing badlands hike with yellow posts to mark the way.

Industry observers note that the Kuwohi Observation Deck atop Great Smoky Mountains National Park offers a bird’s-eye view that’s spot-on for supermoon season. The only catch: You need to arrive early. This tower gets busy, particularly around golden hour. The road in also closes seasonally from December to March, so be prepared to hike if you’re coming for the later supermoons. Other options include the Newfound Gap parking area or the Gatlinburg Scenic Overlook just outside the park.

In a recent development, scenic stop-offs abound along the 30-mile Ross Maxwell Scenic Drive in Big Bend National Park. Several offer great positioning for the supermoon to the northeast. Bookmark Blue Creek Trail, Sotol Vista Overlook, and the Goat Mountain Observation Point. For a near-private show, book a dome at stargazing retreat The Summit at Big Bend near Terlingua; guests can access a secluded hilltop complete with picnic tables, hammocks, and Chihuahuan Desert views.

With fewer crowds and flexibility to drive the Zion Canyon Scenic Drive generally between December and February, winter is one of the best seasons in Zion National Park. It’s even better when a supermoon’s on the horizon. Try Checkerboard Mesa pullout for some of the park’s clearest views to the northeast, or the paved Pa’rus for stellar scenery with the moon illuminating the canyon after it’s risen.

Industry observers note that find the supermoon rising above Malletts Bay from the three-mile Colchester Causeway. This serene perch is especially secluded in winter, as it’s not maintained for bikes. Instead, you can stroll it on foot from its starting point, Causeway Park, to soak up the scenery before driving back to Burlington, just nine miles away.

Admire the lunar sphere from Virginia Beach’s miles of sandy shoreline as it ascends over the Atlantic. Overlooks include Fort Story, home to the 157-foot-tall Cape Henry Lighthouse; Little Island Park from the Sandbridge Fishing Pier; or the Virginia Beach Oceanfront Boardwalk.

Recent findings suggest that rattlesnake Ledge in Washington’s Snoqualmie region is a favorite for sunrises, and the four-mile jaunt is just as impressive during supermoon season. From the peak, you can see Mount Washington, Mount Si, and the surrounding lakes. Expect fewer crowds than peak summer, but winter does bring the chance for ice and snow, so dress appropriately, especially when descending in the dark.

Sources indicate that west Virginia’s only national park brims with supermoon viewpoints. Chief among them is the Grandview Overlook, which peers across the New River’s horseshoe bend. Or get your heart pumping while chasing lunar wonder with a hike on the 2.4-mile Endless Wall Trail; make sure you reach Diamond Point Overlook by moonrise.

Spy the supermoon over Lake Michigan from many public waterfront lookouts in Sheboygan, nicknamed a freshwater surf capital of the world according to Livability.com. There’s North Point Park, kiteboarding haven Sheboygan Kite Beach, and the South Pier, which overlooks the Sheboygan Breakwater Lighthouse.

The prairies stretch to the horizon in Thunder Basin National Grassland, an 875-square-mile ecosystem in northeast Wyoming. These endless views create the perfect recipe for supermoon views. Set trails are few and far between here—most visitors explore cross-country—but some hiking options include the East Upton Trailhead and Kellogg Trailhead in the grassland’s northeast corner.

#9177. Ben Zartman Splices Climbing Slings In His Garage. They’re the Best I’ve Ever Used.
